As Black Friday deals hit Europe, new European Commission data show consumer confidence ranging from cautious optimism in Malta and near-neutral sentiment in Spain to deep gloom in Greece, while Italians cut back sharply on plans for big purchases.

Shop windows across Europe are covered in discount signs today, from Lisbon to Warsaw. Whether people walk in and spend is another matter.

On the same day as Black Friday, the European Commission published its monthly survey of consumers, with a reading for each of the 27 EU countries. It asks households how they feel about their finances, what they expect for the wider economy and how much they plan to spend on big purchases over the next 12 months.

The confidence indicator averages the balances from four questions. A negative reading means negative answers carry more weight overall than positive ones.

For the euro area as a whole, confidence stood at -16.9 in November, confirming last week's early estimate. That is a one-point improvement on October, but still well below the historical average of -10.7.

The backdrop explains much of the caution. Prices in the euro area rose 4% in the year to October, according to Eurostat, the fastest pace since September 2023, driven by energy costs.

Averages hide a lot, though. Country by country, the mood ranges from cautious optimism in Malta to deep pessimism in Greece.

Greece stands alone at the bottom

Greek consumers are by far the gloomiest in the EU. Their confidence reading fell to -50.5 in November from -48.9 in October.

No other country comes close. Romania, the next most pessimistic, stands at -29.7.

Greek households have rarely been cheerful, with a historical average of -40.5. Even so, November's reading sits ten points below that already low bar.

Prices are part of the story. Annual inflation in Greece reached 5.7% in October, the fourth-highest rate in the EU, while Romania recorded the highest at 7%, Eurostat figures show.

After Greece and Romania come Estonia (-29.2), Bulgaria (-28.4), and Italy and Portugal, both at -24.9.

Estonia is the most striking case. Its reading is almost 18 points below the country's own historical average, the widest gap anywhere in the EU.

Italians are holding back on big purchases

For retailers counting on Black Friday, one question in the survey matters more than most. It asks whether households plan to spend more or less on major purchases, such as furniture, appliances or electronics, than they did over the past 12 months.

In Italy, the answer turned sharply more negative. The balance dropped to -46.5 in November from -40.4 in October, far below the country's historical average of -25.1.

Only Romanian households are more reluctant, at -47.4. Greece follows at -43.9.

Italy's overall confidence also slipped to -24.9, its weakest reading in at least a year.

At the other end of the scale, Lithuania (5.0) and Malta (3.4) are the only EU countries where, on balance, households plan to spend more on big purchases over the next 12 months than they did over the past year.

Malta, Spain and Lithuania lead the optimists

Malta is the only EU country with a positive consumer confidence reading, at 2.9.

Spain comes second at -1.1, its best level in at least a year and above its own historical average of -2.4. Lithuania follows closely at -1.4.

Hungary (-5.1) and Sweden (-7.7) complete the top five.

Hungarian consumers tell a different kind of story. Their reading is still negative, but it sits 17 points above the country's historical average of -22.1, the biggest positive gap in the bloc.

In total, eight of the 27 member states now show confidence above their own long-term norms: Malta, Spain, Lithuania, Hungary, Czechia, Luxembourg, Croatia and Poland. Many of them are in central and eastern Europe.

Slovenia sits exactly on its average, while the remaining 18 countries are below theirs.

The big economies sit in the middle

Germany, the EU's largest economy, scored -14.3, a touch better than in October. France improved to -20.2 from -21.9, while the Netherlands slipped to -16.6 from -19.0.

National surveys published earlier this week point to the same cautious mood.

"Lower taxes on fuel are doing little to lift spirits among German consumers," Melanie Debono, senior Europe economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said in a note on Thursday, commenting on the GfK survey of German households.

In France, households grew less worried about their finances and jobs in November, but their willingness to spend on big items weakened further in the INSEE survey.

"The outlook for near-term spending is downbeat, based on these data," Claus Vistesen, chief eurozone economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said in a note on Wednesday.

Saving rather than spending

Across the euro area, households are leaning towards putting money aside. The survey's balance on savings intentions over the next 12 months rose to 10.0 from 8.9, compared with a historical average of -2.9.

Luxembourg leads at 52.6, while in Germany the balance rose to 23.2 from 20.8.

There is one piece of better news for shops. Consumers' expectations for price rises eased. The balance on price expectations for the next 12 months eased to 30.0 from 33.8 in the euro area, although it remains well above its average of 21.4.

The wider picture is not one of collapse. The Commission's broader economic sentiment indicator, which also covers businesses, fell to 95.8 in the euro area, dragged down by industry.

"Down sharply, but recession risks remain low," Vistesen said in a note on Friday.

For Europe's retailers, that may be the real Black Friday problem. Consumers are not in crisis, but many of them are in no hurry to spend.

After a a decade-long transformation costing more than €500 million, London Museum reopens its doors this weekend at the former Victorian General Market at Smithfield and it's billing itself as the world's largest city museum.

During the long and often torturous process of refurbishing the once derelict Smithfield meat market, the London Museum director Sharon Ament said her intention was to create a building that represented the city in all it's "colourful and complicated glory."

Her vision of the British capital's past is now ready for the public to render its verdict.

For starters, the €532 million building replaces the poorly located Museum of London which closed in 2002. The new version is much easier to find and reach by public transport. In fact, visitors to the historic site can even see passing trains, as it allows free and largely unfettered access to people living and working around the building.

"It has lots of entrances so unlike many museums, there are few barriers to getting in and out. And even if people just flow through the museum on their way to work, that is good enough for me," Ament says.

Moving an established museum to a new location was no small undertaking, but the attraction of Smithfield proved difficult to resist, according to Ament: "Museum leaders don't really think about moving a museum. It's not for the faint hearted, I would say, but the compelling attraction of Smithfield Market... You know, I could see its potential as a forum museum and to be a really great museum."

Past Time paradise

The museum draws on a collection of around seven million objects gathered from across London's boroughs, telling the story of the capital and its inhabitants across thousands of years.

Billing itself as the world's largest city museum, it features diverse items ranging from Roman mosaics, the swimming trunks of London Olympic hero Tom Daely, a bagel filled with barbecued pork, and a sewer-clogging chunk of fat.

The redevelopment has also restored Smithfield's historic General Market, preserving its sweeping dome, decorative ironwork and vaulted brick cellars while creating a new exhibition space.

The former meat market's architecture has also helped shape the museum's new approach. Its large trading floor and extensive underground spaces offer opportunities to bring London's history to life in different ways.

"So we found that a market makes a brilliant museum. It's made for public to come in and out, it's got deep basements, and then it's set in this historic area. So it's enabled us to tell the story of that area as well," explains Ament.

Ament's ambitions for the new museum extend beyond traditional expectations. She plans to use the now all too commonplace immersive projections and spatial sound to bring Roman London to life in its underground vaults. But, Ament also wants the new building to become a lively social space, with cultural events, storytelling activities and late-night openings featuring DJs on Friday and Saturday nights.

For Ament, it's crucial that museums today respond to changing expectations and become places where people can gather. "We've learnt that people need places to gather. We've learned that history is not something to be frightened of. And, you know, sometimes it's tough and sometimes it's glorious. Let's talk about that balance."

The permanent galleries will be free to enter, allowing visitors to explore London's history without paying an admission fee.

London Museum opens on 28 November, with further exhibition and learning spaces planned as part of a second phase of redevelopment in 2028.

The EU summit on the Union's common budget for 2028-2034 has initially failed. Some want to protect established spending, others to cut costs and mainly finance new strategic tasks, warns foreign policy expert Alexander Wolf of the Hanns Seidel Foundation in Berlin.

Europe wants to become more independent, competitive and secure. Yet it is precisely the tasks that are crucial to this that face the deepest cuts in the draft for the next EU budget. Behind this lies a structural problem in European politics.

The special Brussels summit on the European budget for the years 2028 to 2034 ended without agreement. On 17 December, the heads of state and government will meet again. Until then, the main question will be how much Europe is prepared to spend.

Costa wants cuts above all in new strategic priorities

The European Commission has proposed a financial framework of just under €2 trillion. Council President António Costa has reduced this to around €1.78 trillion. Germany and other net contributors still consider that too high.

More revealing than the overall figure, however, is where Costa makes the cuts. Compared with the Commission’s draft, he removes around €95.5 billion from competitiveness, prosperity and security, and around €54 billion from agriculture, cohesion and related tasks. That amounts to reductions of 16 and 5% respectively. In defence industry, security and space, the cuts are almost 30%.

Costa’s draft does foresee substantial increases for defence and competitiveness compared with the current budget. Even so, the new strategic priorities are being cut disproportionately.

The logic of national interests

Germany and other net contributors want to limit their payments and focus the budget more strongly on competitiveness and security. Poland and other cohesion countries defend the funding for their regions. France wants an ambitious European budget while also protecting its agriculture. Italy takes a sceptical view of additional European levies.

Each of these positions is understandable from a national perspective. The problem arises from how they interact.

The European financial framework requires unanimity in the Council and the consent of the European Parliament. Every government can make its approval conditional on its own interests being safeguarded. This favours spending whose benefits can be clearly attributed to individual member states.

A French president can explain to farmers which subsidies he has secured in Brussels. A Polish prime minister can point to new roads and modernised regions. But which head of government can claim the benefit of a joint European air defence system purely for his or her own country?

Joint European tasks do have political advocates. But their benefits are less easily mapped onto the national balance sheet that underpins almost every budget negotiation in the end: how much did we pay in, and how much do we get back?

Agriculture or defence? A budget for a new world

About 60% of the current European financial framework is devoted to agriculture and cohesion. Both areas serve core purposes of European integration: food security, economic development and the reduction of regional disparities.

However, Europe now has additional tasks to tackle that did not carry anything like the same weight when this budget structure was created.

Russia is threatening Europe’s security order. China has built up significant technological and industrial capacity in strategic sectors. The United States is pursuing its own economic and security interests, which do not necessarily coincide with Europes.

The conditions under which the bloc has built its prosperity in recent decades are changing fundamentally.

That cannot be addressed simply through higher national defence spending. It is equally about joint defence research, industrial production capacity, secure supply chains, cross-border energy networks, military mobility and European expertise in key technologies.

In 2024 Mario Draghi set out what would be needed: catching up the innovation gap with the United States and China, combining decarbonisation with competitiveness, and strengthening Europe’s security by reducing strategic dependencies. He put the additional private and public investment required at €750 to 800 billion a year.

This sum cannot and should not be financed solely from the European budget. However, the budget can mobilise national and private investment and make joint projects possible where individual member states cannot achieve the necessary scale on their own.

The substance is shrinking: what Europe should finance jointly

I believe the European budget should be shaped much more by its tasks. The decisive factor should be what the member states can achieve better, more efficiently or more cheaply together than alone.

Agriculture and the less developed regions of Europe still need reliability. But their shares of the budget should, with appropriate transition periods, gradually yet clearly decline in order to create more scope for joint investment in the future.

Anyone who thinks Europe can simply carry on as before is living off a substance that is steadily shrinking. A Europe that wants to become more sovereign and more independent also has to get ahead of events.

That calls for honesty on the revenue side. Costa’s draft sets aside €158 billion solely for repaying the EU debt taken on during the pandemic. This money is not available for other tasks.

Costa therefore proposes additional European sources of revenue, including levies on digital services provided by large companies, on tobacco and on non-recycled electronic waste. Anyone who rejects additional own resources has to explain whether they prefer higher national contributions or corresponding cuts. And anyone who demands more European tasks has to say how they should be funded.

The contribution rebates also belong in this context. They are the expression of a budget logic that measures the success of European policy by national returns. As long as this calculation dominates, funding joint tasks will remain structurally more difficult.

The price of an agreement: established or new tasks?

Germany and France are pushing for an understanding before the end of the year. Given the French presidential election next spring, that is understandable.

One possible compromise would be an even smaller overall volume combined with concessions to the net contributors, agriculture and the cohesion countries. Particularly contentious sources of revenue could be postponed, and funding for further aid to Ukraine could be negotiated separately.

Such an agreement would carry weight. It would create planning certainty and show that 27 governments, despite differing interests, are capable of reaching a compromise.

The crucial question, however, would be the price at which it is achieved. If the main effect is to protect established spending while once again making the new strategic tasks bear most of the savings, the underlying problem would remain.

Europe would still have to tackle many of its new tasks largely through national budgets, loans and additional financing instruments. Especially for long term investment in security, infrastructure and technological competitiveness, a lack of joint planning can lead to higher costs and avoidable duplication.

We do not have to turn all our challenges into European ones. But we should organise and fund at European level those we can no longer adequately handle at national level.

Anyone who wants a more sovereign and more independent Europe must also be prepared to draw fiscal policy conclusions from that.

Unlike most pooches, Eba spends her days on a boat - assisting scientists in the fight to save dwindling killer whale populations.

There's no time to play fetch or sniff around the park for a dog like Eba - she's too busy saving endangered orcas in the wild.

The 11-year-old pooch works alongside Dr Deborah Giles, who has been tracking the dwindling population of Southern Resident killer whales for years.

These orcas are spending less time in the Salish Sea, the maze of inland waters between Washington State and British Columbia in the US as they search desperately for food.

But in the last half-decade, the orcas have been hunting coho and chum salmon just north of Seattle during the autumn.

It's providing an opportunity for collaboration between The SeaDoc Society and the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance who are using drones mounted with petri dishes and microscope slides to collect droplets from whale spouts.

How Eba the dog helps protect orcas

The team crams into the small boat and motors fast to where Giles’ contacts have reported sightings. With the orcas in view, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance drone pilot and senior scientist James Sheppard launches the drone from the boat’s bow.

He hovers high first to hone in on a whale’s location, then drops to just a dozen or so feet above the surface. He focuses on an adult male with a massive dorsal fin punching through the water.

The spout spray reaches about 1.8 to 3 meters into the air, and it’s as wide as a basketball, Sheppard says. As the whale breathes, the drone sweeps horizontally across the falling droplets.

“Once we’ve got the sample it’s important we bring the drone back to the boat as quickly as possible so that the samples don’t get degraded with the wind and the sunlight,” Sheppard said.

The conditions on this November day prove difficult. With less sunlight, the whales are harder to see, and they’re foraging and surfacing unpredictably.

They pay little mind to the drone, which is also equipped with cameras to record video and infrared sensors to capture a whale’s body temperature.

“The few times that they’ve actually noticed the drone they’ll just roll on their side, maybe look at it for a few seconds, and then just keep on swimming. To them, it’s just a strange seagull that’s been following them for a few seconds,” said Sheppard.

After the drone, it’s Eba’s turn. The 11-year-old dog heads straight to the bow and sniffs the air, her head sticking out beyond the boat.

She’s held on a leash by Jim Rappold, Giles’ husband and research partner. Eba picks up a scent, lets out a few whines and paces on the bow to alert her finding. But on this day, her human handlers couldn’t find the feces she smelled.

Scientists use feces to create health profiles for orcas

Over the years, the team has collected hundreds of fecal and breath samples. Those contain hormonal, bacterial, fungal, parasitic, and DNA information that is sent to the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance lab for analysis.

The data is then compiled to create health profiles for individual orcas.

“If we need to intervene, if we need to have a discussion about something that might need to happen to an individual animal, we have that animal’s entire record right there,” Giles says..

By comparing pregnancy hormones in females over time, researchers have found many are having miscarriages. That’s in addition to a high calf mortality rate, as illustrated by mothers seen carrying dead calves.

The plight of the Southern Resident killer whales stands in contrast with their cousins that share these waters.

Bigg’s killer whales are thriving. They eat sea mammals like seals, sea lions and porpoises, which are plentiful in the Salish Sea. Some of their females are having calves every two years, Giles explains. Gestation alone takes 17-18 months.

While authorities have taken steps to help the whales like reducing vessel noise, Giles argues that the most important action is restoring salmon runs.

Salmon that spawn in the Salish Sea can travel as far north as Alaska, where they are caught, preventing them from returning to where the orcas can intercept them.

“It’s our job to turn back the clock,” she says.

Officers have complained of shifts lasting up to 15 hours and prolonged periods away from their families.

The current unrest has compounded grievances that have been building for years.

From the 2015 terrorist attacks and the prolonged Yellow Vest protests of 2018 and 2019 to successive waves of social unrest, French police forces have been repeatedly mobilised on a large scale.

“Never any respite. But we've never given up,” said Landreau.

He pointed in particular to the shortage of forensic police personnel, numbering just 3,300 nationwide, despite their increasingly important role in criminal investigations.

“We've moved from a culture of confession to a culture of evidence,” he said. “From minor burglaries to terrorist attacks, they're the ones on the front line.”

Aris, who holds British citizenship through his late father, academic Michael Aris, said he had run a proof-of-life campaign last year, and that the Red Cross visited her earlier this year and confirmed she was alive.

"They call this house arrest, but I do not call this a house arrest. She's not in her own home. She's allowed no access to any sort of media, as far as I'm aware," Aris said.

Analiza sistemelor hidrologice globale, realizată în cadrul unui proiect de colaborare condus de Academia Chineză de Științe, a relevat că volumul apei dulci de suprafață de pe planetă a scăzut drastic în cei doi ani, care au fost cei mai călduroși din istoria înregistrărilor. Debitele râurilor au scăzut cu -5,7% sub nivelul normal, iar volumul de apă stocat în lacuri și rezervoare a scăzut cu -9,5%, fiind cea mai mare scădere sincronizată a apei de suprafață înregistrată cel puțin din 1991. 

Cercetătorii arată că, pe măsură ce planeta se încălzește, ciclul apei devine tot mai extrem, O atmosferă mai caldă extrage mai multă umiditate din soluri, râuri și lacuri, iar solul mai fierbinte accelerează și mai mult evaporarea. Umiditatea se transformă apoi în ploi torențiale în alte zone, adesea asupra oceanelor, provocând oscilații mai accentuate între secetă și inundații. Astfel, în perioada 2023-2024, râurile au avut un debit redus chiar li în zonele afectate de inundații severe.

Analiza a combinat măsurătorile debitului din 150 dintre cele mai importante bazine hidrografice ale lumii cu date satelitare care au monitorizat 1,2 milioane de lacuri și rezervoare. Datele au fost obținute între 1991 și 2025.

Sulagna Mishra, unul dintre autorii studiului, a declarat: “Rezultatele evidențiază un paradox important al schimbărilor climatice: o atmosferă mai caldă nu înseamnă neapărat că este disponibilă mai multă apă pe uscat. America de Sud a înregistrat cele mai pronunțate scăderi. Debitul râurilor a scăzut cu -17,8% iar lacurile și barajele cu -16,5%, chiar și în zonele afectate de precipitatii extreme și inundații. 

Resursele de apă din întreaga lume se confruntă cu numeroase amenințări, printre care fenomenul “super El Niño”, secete provocate de criza climatică, poluare și supraexploatare.

Named one of the European Capitals of Tourism for 2027, Ljubljana offers travellers riverside cafés, historic landmarks and traditional cuisine. Here’s why you should visit the Slovenian capital.

Ljubljana was named one of the 2027 European Capitals of Tourism by the European Commission, earning the top spot in the category for cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants.

The jury was especially impressed with the city’s “commitment to knowledge sharing, continuous learning and resident-focused initiatives”, with the European Commission adding that it has an “ambitious programme of activities planned for 2027”.

If you’re curious about travelling to the Slovenian capital and finding out what there is to see and do, here’s all you need to know.

The city’s ‘lounge’ along the river

The Visit Ljubljana tourism board describes the embankments of the Ljubljanica River as the heart of the capital’s social scene – “densely scattered with lively cafés offering outdoor seating”.

The scenic riverbanks have a history dating back to Roman times and are an important archaeological site, where excavations have uncovered objects from prehistory to the early modern period.

It is also ideal for adventure tourists, especially during the summer when the city centre can be explored by stand-up paddleboard or by joining a guided kayak tour.

An ideal destination for a stroll or ride

For travellers looking to stretch their legs, Ljubljana’s compact size and car-free old town are ideal for exploring on foot or by bike.

The city’s historic centre sits along the Ljubljanica River, a stone’s throw away from Prešeren Square. Here, visitors will find a monument to Slovenian poet, France Prešeren, as well as the nearby Triple Bridge. Its stairways on each side of the bridges lead to terraces filled with poplar trees along the river.

In the old town itself, visitors can stroll to the Central Market, which combines indoor and open marketplaces within a striking colonnade. Fruits, balcony flowers, local cheeses and dry-cured meats are among the produce on offer, and in the indoor venue there is a fish market with a small restaurant.

Overlooking the old town, Ljubljana Castle sits atop Castle Hill, just a short climb from the city centre. Perched at an elevation of 400 metres above sea level, its history spans around 900 years, with the landmark now being home to exhibitions and cultural events year-round.

Other attractions and landmarks

While strolling in the city, these are some must-visit spots to add to your itinerary.

For an insight into the architect who moulded Ljubljana’s cityscape, make a beeline for Plečnik House. The complex comprises two houses that once belonged to Slovenian architect, Jože Plečnik – the marvel behind the city’s National and University Library as well as the Church of St. Michael.

The complex displays his original sketches, plans, photographs and models of his creations, including projects that never came to fruition.

The National Gallery is a hub for historical art, holding the country’s largest collection of fine art from the High Middle Ages to the 20th-century. Its permanent collection is made up of nearly 600 works by Slovenian and European artists, including a permanent exhibition by Slovenian modernist painter, Zoran Mušič.

The Dragon Bridge, adorned with four statues of the mythical creature, was constructed from 1900 to 1901. The bridge across the Ljubljanica River is a scenic spot for taking holiday snaps.

Where to stay

The city has no shortage of hotels and accommodation options.

At InterContinental Ljubljana, visitors can choose from 165 rooms and larger suites. The one-bedroom suite with castle views features a cosy fireplace, private sauna and a separate area for dining. Located on the 19th floor, it also offers panoramic views of the city. Guests can unwind at the Serenity Spa & Gym and also sample Slovene cuisine at its B-Restaurant.

Aside from hotels and hostels, visitors can opt to stay at a holiday farm. Located just outside of the city, Pri Lazarju tourist farm is more than 300 years old and offers guests the chance to experience farm life. Beyond its scenic surroundings, guests can get involved in barn and pasture work and take guided tours of local landmarks, including the Besnica River, or hike along the Borovničeva trail.

Meanwhile, Ljubljana Resort Hotel & Camp is the only campsite within the capital, situated just five kilometres north of the city centre. The vast site extends across three acres and is situated by the River Sava. Along the river, guests can enjoy outdoor activities, including fly fishing. The wider complex also features hotel accommodation, complete with an outdoor swimming pool, fitness centre, beach volleyball courts and a restaurant.

Slovenian cuisine to try

Slovenia’s culinary traditions have developed over centuries, with much of the traditional fare being served in “gostilnas”, which are family-run restaurants where classic dishes are served.

What has been coined as a “typical Ljubljana lunch” dates back to the 19th century, when locals would visit a gostilna on the city’s outskirts on the weekends. The meal has changed little since then. Popular dishes include boiled beef tongue and traditional “bleki” noodles in a soup. Another lunch class is Vodnik's lamb's lettuce salad from Valentin Vodnik's “Kuharske bukve” (The Cookbook), which was published in 1799 as the first cookbook ever written in Slovenian.

Another popular dish, “Leteči žganci”, or flying “žganci”, harks back to the 17th-century. Made from fried chicken legs and wings, it was popularised by workers at the town port by the Ljubljana River. According to Visit Ljubljana, žganci itself is an “everyday dish of boiled flour commonly associated with poverty and struggle for survival".

Meanwhile, since 2013, the city’s “Odprta kuhna”, or open kitchen, has become a popular culinary staple, taking place in the Pogačarjev Trg Square. The food market opens every Friday from March to October annually, bringing Slovenian cuisine, international eateries, sweet treats and even artisanal crafts.

Ljubljana and its surroundings also have a strong presence in the Michelin Guide, with 20 selected restaurants. The Guide described Gostilna na Gradu, which offers traditional cuisine, as being "worth queuing for", especially for its location in Ljubljana Castle's vast inner courtyard.

„Gianina e mult mai deșteaptă și mai educată decât lasă să se vadă”

Ai lucrat cu Radu la „Dracula”, iar atunci când ți-a spus despre un nou proiect la care lucrează, i-ai spus în glumă că și tu vorbești franceză. Ulterior ai primit scenariul și te-ai prezentat la casting. Ai povestit în mai multe rânduri despre cum ai aprofundat franceza timp de opt ore pe zi, de-a lungul a doar câteva luni, și cum ai învățat foarte bine scenariul, însă cum ai descrie-o pe Gianina, personajul tău, celor care încă nu o cunosc?

Haha, da, l-am cam mințit pe Radu. Până la urmă i-am mărturisit, i s-a părut amuzant și cumva a apreciat că am avut curajul să-i spun. Acum vorbesc (sper) foarte ok franceza și mă bucur că am rămas cu asta în urma proiectului, deși n-am mai folosit-o de când am terminat (râde). 

Pentru mine, Gianina e mult mai deșteaptă și mai educată decât lasă să se vadă. Asta pentru că e periculos pentru o femeie în situația ei să comenteze prea mult. Astfel că, acceptând, zâmbind și spunând că nu se pricepe ea prea mult la politică, de fapt, își protejează locul. 

Referitor la experiența alături de Radu Jude și la faptul că ai spus că „lucrul cu Radu te îmbogățește”, cum a fost să lucrezi alături de el? Ce ai învățat nou sau ce te-a provocat să înveți nou?

E un om extrem de inteligent, cu o cultură incredibilă, și am învățat enorm de la el. 

Datorită lui am descoperit-o pe poeta Victoria Chang și tot de la el am aflat ce mare fan al lui John Cage este, pe care l-am descoperit atunci, și pe care acum îl ador. Și când spun incredibilă nu mă refer doar la faptul că știe niște pictori sau niște autori de renume: cunoaște autori contemporani, avangardiști, are niște referințe de cinema pe care nu le-am mai auzit de la nimeni. 

Pentru mine, ca persoană extrem de curioasă și pasionată de astfel de lucruri, a fost o experiență extraordinară și îmi doresc să stau în preajma lui ca artist. Cât despre lucrul propriu-zis cu el, am devenit mai profesionistă, pentru că el știe foarte bine ce vrea și trebuie să te calibrezi foarte repede la viziunea lui. Am învățat să înțeleg mai bine un concept, o cheie de joc, și să le aplic rapid, iar asta cred că m-a pregătit mai bine pentru proiectele viitoare. 

Pe lângă asta, mi-a lărgit considerabil cultura cinematografică, pentru că e cu adevărat pasionat de cinema. A fost doar o lună de lucru la acest proiect, dar și la „Dracula” am învățat foarte multe despre cinema și mă simt mai bogată cultural.

Privind filmul în ansamblul său, care consideri că sunt principalele teme și ce ți-ar plăcea să ajungă la oameni odată cu povestea asta?

Wow! Radu e un om extrem de complex, care știe atât de multe lucruri și are o minte atât de bogată. Și sunt atât de multe lucruri în film care pot scăpa cu ușurință cuiva care nu prinde referințele. 

Menționez câteva care poate nu sunt evidente: asemănarea intenționată cu celebrul film al lui Chantal Akerman, „Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles” (1975), și de aici tema vieții care se scurge pe lângă tine, o juxtapunere pe care o face și prin povestea „Tinerețe fără bătrânețe și viață fără de moarte”, care se regăsește în film. 

De asemenea, paralela cu „Jurnalul unei cameriste”, romanul lui Mirbeau după care filmul e liber inspirat, un roman extrem de sexy chiar și pentru zilele noastre, pe care Radu îl folosește atât pentru fragmentele în care Gianina joacă teatru, cât și pentru paralela cu persoana care nu are neapărat un trecut clar, care minte ca să supraviețuiască. 

Și, desigur, tema trecutului colonial al Franței, care se perpetuează în continuare prin capitalism. 

Legat de aspectul migrației și al româncelor care pleacă la muncă în străinătate, în timp ce copiii lor rămân acasă, în grija bunicilor, ce ai înțeles mai clar despre această realitate prin rolul Gianinei?

Mi s-a părut interesant că au existat oameni care mi-au spus că sunt prea tânără sau că arăt prea cool ca să interpretez un astfel de personaj. Și, de fapt, asta e și ideea: un personaj care arată ca mine poate foarte bine să facă muncă de îngrijire în vestul Europei. Poate fi oricare dintre noi. Singura diferență e privilegiul financiar. Nimic altceva nu ne deosebește.

„Tema cea mai sensibilă mi se pare trecerea timpului”

Cum a fost pentru tine să lucrezi o lună în Franța, alături de o echipă formată din francezi? Care sunt aspectele care au ieșit în evidență în lucrul cu ei, în comparație cu modul de lucru al românilor?

Sunt, în mod evident, mult mai bine pregătiți și, surprinzător, extrem de bine educați în ceea ce privește cinemaul și istoria lui. Au niște referințe culturale pe care, de exemplu, oamenii din domeniul nostru nu le au. 

Ca să compar cele două situații, aș spune că diferența majoră e că majoritatea oamenilor din echipele de la noi s-au format la Buftea: oameni care nu vin dintr-un mediu artistic, nu au facultate în domeniu și au început să lucreze pur și simplu pentru că locuiau în Buftea. A fost mai degrabă o chestiune de context decât una de pasiune. 

Pe tine ce te-a sensibilizat cel mai mult la film și la personajul tău?

Foarte puțin previzibil, m-a sensibilizat povestea „Tinerețe fără bătrânețe” și nici acum nu-mi explic neapărat de ce. 

Eu, care plâng foarte tehnic ca actriță, am simțit, una dintre puținele dăți din viața mea, că plâng cu adevărat în timp ce spuneam textul din scena respectivă. Mi s-a părut foarte interesant și cred că e exact din același motiv pentru care tema cea mai sensibilă mi se pare trecerea timpului, pe care nu-l poți opri, și imponderabilitatea lui. 

„Nu pot să spun că îmi aleg proiectele. Fac ce vine”

Spuneai că la noi în țară actorii nu-și prea aleg proiectele. De ce crezi că se întâmplă asta și ce s-ar putea sau ți-ar plăcea să se schimbe pentru ca lucrurile să fie diferite?

Cred cu adevărat că nu ne alegem proiectele sau că nu suntem în poziția de a ne alege proiectele. Și nu prea cred pe nimeni care spune că își alege proiectele, decât dacă are deja o susținere financiară solidă. Atunci, sigur, poate să aleagă în funcție de diverși factori. Pentru mine asta nu există, adică nu pot să spun că îmi aleg proiectele. Fac ce vine. Sigur, sunt proiecte care îmi plac mult și altele pe care le fac doar pentru bani. Și cred că e ceva firesc. 

Vreau să ne oprim puțin și asupra industriei de film din România din prezent. În opinia ta, ce funcționează și cum te raportezi la filmele românești din ultimii ani, și unde crezi că e loc de mai bine?

Mă bucur enorm că se întâmplă acest val al filmului comercial, chiar dacă nu îl consum și nu e ceva ce-mi doresc să văd, pentru că tocmai asta ridică industria în ansamblu. Chiar Radu spunea că industria de film franceză e cea mai mare din Europa și a doua după Hollywood, pentru că francezii fac extrem de multe filme. Cele mai multe sunt proaste, dar dintr-un volum atât de mare, evident că și procentul filmelor bune va fi mult mai mare. Așa că mă bucur că, în general, în România se produc mai multe filme. 

E însă foarte trist ce se întâmplă cu Centrul Național al Cinematografiei și cu moartea clinică în care se află, dar, în general, cultural vorbind, România nu stă deloc extraordinar. 

Ce mi-ar plăcea foarte mult să văd ar fi o mai bună accesibilizare pentru persoanele cu dizabilități și pentru cele cu deficiențe de auz, atât în filme, cât și în rândul celor care lucrează în domeniul cinematografic. Aș vrea să văd subiectul abordat mai des și sălile de cinema mai accesibile. 

M-ar bucura, de asemenea, să văd cultura romă pusă mai în valoare. Deși se întâmplă câteva lucruri în teatru, de pildă compania Giuvlipen, iar actrița și regizoarea Alina Șerban a avut succesul pe care l-a avut cu filmul ei de debut la Veneția, tot cred că avem nevoie de o discuție mai amplă despre această cultură, care e extraordinar de bogată și de interesantă. 

„Sunt genul de actriță care nu e neapărat fan al aplauzelor de pe scenă”

„Jurnalul unei cameriste” a integrat, sub forma unor scenete, și pasaje din cartea lui Mirbeau. Cum vezi legătura dintre teatru și film și ce te atrage mai mult dintre cele două? De ce?

Pe mine personal mă atrage mai mult filmul și cred că e și un rezultat al experienței mele: până în acest punct am lucrat ceva mai mult în film decât în teatru, iar aici mă simt mai confortabil, înțeleg mai bine. Toate referințele mele sunt de cinema și poate mai puțin de teatru. 

Teatrul, se știe, a evoluat din ritual, iar la André Bazin am citit că filmul vine din pictură și, mai departe, din fotografie. Apoi am dat peste un reel care spunea că filmul va evolua către inteligența artificială și mi-am zis că, de fapt, ar putea fi concluzia logică a acestui drum. Recunosc, gândul ăsta mă sperie puțin, dar, în același timp, dacă asta e evoluția firească, let it be (las-o așa, n.r.). 

Mie îmi place mai mult filmul, mai ales în cazul celui românesc: consider că nivelul filmului românesc e foarte ridicat, suntem apreciați la nivel mondial, și pe bună dreptate. 

Din păcate, nu cred că teatrul românesc e, în momentul de față, la nivelul filmului. 

Apropo de asta, după ce ai intrat în contact cu cartea autorului francez, publicată în urmă cu 126 de ani, o vezi ca pe o lectură încă actuală în realitatea din prezent sau cum te raportezi la ea?

Da, mi se pare o lectură extrem de interesantă, sexy, feministă, o carte superbă, și îmi pare rău că n-o știam dinainte. E extrem de actuală, lucru îmbucurător pentru un autor atât de vizionar, dar și trist, pentru că patriarhatul nu s-a schimbat prea mult. 

Filmul a avut un parcurs festivalier foarte bun și a fost ovaționat minute întregi la Cannes. Cum ai perceput reacția publicului internațional față de această poveste și, din discuțiile purtate, care a fost feedbackul pe care l-ai primit?

Nu știu exact cum să mă raportez la reacția publicului. Sunt genul de actriță care nu e neapărat fan al aplauzelor de pe scenă și, în general, nu prea știu cum să mă raportez la ele. Cred, oricum, că felul în care privim și înțelegem un film sau orice produs artistic ține foarte mult de cine ești tu, de bagajul tău emoțional, de felul în care ai experimentat lumea până în acel moment. Și cred că toate reacțiile, fie ele pozitive sau negative, sunt valide. 

Cât despre publicul internațional, m-am bucurat mult că s-a scris foarte bine, dar, din nou, cred că ține de un cumul de factori și e ceva extrem de personal. Mă bucur enorm pentru Radu, pentru că îmi place foarte mult ce face ca artist, și mă bucur că s-a scris bine și despre mine și că nu l-am dezamăgit public. 

„Avem prea puțini copii educați cu adevărat în România și e vina sistemului”

Într-un interviu pe care l-ai acordat recent, legat de rolul social sau politic al unui astfel de film, spuneai că la noi nu vedem politicieni în sala de cinema și că „sălile noastre sunt goale la filme românești”. De ce crezi că, în 2026, când multe filme românești au avut succes și ecouri internaționale, oamenii tot nu vin să le vadă?

Cred că oamenii încă nu vin la cinema pentru că nu sunt obișnuiți. Nu s-a format acest obicei. Cred și că un public inteligent și cunoscător intră în contact cu cinemaul de la vârste fragede, măcar din liceu sau din facultate, iar în general predispoziția e spre filmele comerciale. Dar e posibil să fie doar impresia mea: când merg la cinema, de multe ori observ că suntem doar

două persoane în sală, eu și persoana cu care am venit. Poate e doar experiența mea și mă înșel, iar sălile sunt, de fapt, pline. Sper să fie așa.

Ce ți-ar plăcea să se schimbe, fie în privința interesului publicului, fie în privința implicării autorităților sau a statului în promovarea filmelor românești, astfel încât filmele care prezintă realități ale lumii în care trăim și atrag atenția asupra lor să poată fi valorificate la adevăratul lor potențial?

E o problemă mult mai amplă, iar ce descrie întrebarea ta e un simptom, nu problema în sine. 

Cred că ar trebui să mergem mult mai în profunzime, până la felul în care se raportează autoritățile la educație în România. Cred că în școli nu există niciun fel de interes pentru promovarea culturii încă din clasele primare: în continuare, excursiile copiilor din mediul rural sunt la mall, în continuare se studiază pe manuale învechite, în continuare singurul scop educațional e bacalaureatul. De aici pornește problema. Până să ajungem la un public adult care merge la cinema, avem nevoie de instituții care să promoveze cultura pentru copii, încă din clasele primare. Și când spun cultură mă refer la tot: la pictură, la artă, la cinema. 

Mi se pare că avem prea puțini copii educați cu adevărat în România și chiar cred că e vina sistemului.

Popularitatea rolului din film a schimbat ceva pentru tine? La ce alte proiecte lucrezi în prezent?

Nu știu dacă schimbă ceva. Cum spuneam și mai sus, cred că niciun proiect și nicio colaborare nu-ți garantează existența în industrie. După ce ai terminat de filmat un proiect și după ce acesta s-a lansat, ești din nou în punctul zero, și cred că asta e valabil pentru toți actorii. Nu știu dacă i se întâmplă cuiva, poate la un nivel mult mai înalt, să fie sunat să joace într-un proiect fără casting. Mie nu mi s-a întâmplat: am dat casting pentru toate proiectele în care am lucrat.

Iar popularitatea asta e ceva ce dispare după o lună, două maximum. Tocmai am terminat de filmat un rol principal într-un thriller regizat de cineastul polonez Michał Sznekiak, o coproducție Moldova-Polonia, și un rol secundar în filmul lui Octav Chelaru, pe care îl ador, „O fată singură în noapte”. 

Am lucrat recent și cu Bogdan Mirică și urmează să am un rol mic în următorul film al lui Radu. Ce cred e că, odată cu experiența și cu validarea care mi-a venit din exterior, am căpătat mai multă încredere, așa că am început să merg și la castinguri mai încrezătoare.

Nostalgia and nihilism collide in David Fincher's gritty but edgeless follow-up to Quentin Tarantino's 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood'.

The year is 1977, and the movies ain’t what they used to be.

Over the last decade, a New Wave of young filmmakers have taken over, moving from indoor sets to city streets to film grittier, meaner, counter-cultural stories that reflect the disillusionment of the times.

In the process, Hollywood’s prior artifice has been shattered; no longer a glossy, well-oiled machine solely controlled by big studios. 

But nothing lasts forever — and something is about to come along (as it always does) that once again changes everything: Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope. 

As screenwriter and filmmaker Paul Schrader told film historian Peter Biskind for his book "Easy Riders and Raging Bulls": “Star Wars was the film that ate the heart and the soul of Hollywood. It created the big-budget comic book mentality.”

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (TFMCB) takes place in the summer of ‘77, right at the height of Star Wars mania. While only glimpsed on cinema marquees in passing shots, its background presence sets the tone for a movie that’s not only wrestling with shifting attitudes and the violent tug of time, but also itself.

A follow up to Quentin Tarantino’s Oscar-winning Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019), TFMCB focuses on its character Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt), the former stuntman to actor Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) who once kicked Bruce Lee’s a** and took down a bunch of Manson Family members while high on an acid soaked cigarette.

In other words, Cliff is cool. That's kind of his whole thing.

Eight years later, he’s living with his dad (Peter Weller) and working multiple jobs in Los Angeles: a projectionist at the New Beverley Cinema, a cocktail maker at a bar with mud fighting contests, and a “fixer” for celebrities being blackmailed by criminals.

Oh, and he also sometimes acts in porno movies under the stag name Randy.

The plot mostly hinges around Cliff’s relationship with an excitable TV actor named Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), who finds himself in a spot of trouble with some Filipino gangsters that are now threatening to kill his wife (Carla Gugino).

But mis-adventures aside,TFMCB is primarily a hangout movie.

Similar to George Lucas's American Graffiti, it excels at immersing viewers in retro Americana — albeit a crumpled and nonchalant version. As we ride with Cliff through the streets of LA, the staticky sounds of KRLA radio station a near-constant presence, you can almost smell the tobacco smoke wafting through the screen and it's just fun soaking up the atmosphere, slouching into it like a weathered chair.

Booth himself is as engaging as ever and manages to maintain some of his enigma despite being front and centre. This is thanks to Pitt's endearing performance, which once again leans into the character's effortless bad-a**ery — part surfer-dude, part grindhouse hunk.

But if Once upon a Time was Tarantino’s ode to a golden age of cinema - a re-writing of history with a fairy tale ending - TFMCB is a cynical reckoning with reality and the inevitability of change.

While Cliff confronts this by coasting on his own legends and clinging to the fringes of an increasingly loose-moralled industry, he knows no happy ending is coming — and who cares? None of it “means sh**” to him anyway.

Director David Fincher (Seven, Gone Girl) was the perfect choice for capturing such apathy, dipping Tarantino’s script in a vat of slick gloom that sharpens and darkens the mood. And it is at points very dark — both in its on-screen brutalities, and its visuals, which swap Once upon a Time's vibrant 35mm film for the dirge of desaturated digital.

Still, the nostalgic vibes of its predecessor remain, and anyone with an interest in this particular era of Hollywood filmmaking history will find themselves drawn to its niche cultural references and rich world building; scenes bathed in neon sleaze and analogue media ASMR.

Beyond the movie’s cool persona, however, there’s not much substance to hold onto.

Cliff Booth is a great character, but what made him so beloved in Once upon a Time was his bond with Rick specifically and his interactions with other equally-charismatic characters. In TFMCB, there are very few interesting characters to anchor him in the same way. The criminals are bothersome but bland, Peter Weller as Gus Booth is woefully underused, and TV star Charlie Peters is eccentric in an oddly underwhelming way.

The most compelling on-screen dynamic is between Cliff and the glamazonian Hollywood agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), who share a memorable scene on a balcony discussing the terms and conditions of Cliff’s slapping kink. But the chemistry between the two tends to simmer more than sizzle, and Crosby, outside of a fun speech about movies being like cheeseburgers, is mostly relegated to solemn looks and the occasional burst of sass.

Meanwhile, a lack of overall narrative purpose means that Cliff meanders from moment to moment, which can be compelling in its own way, but lessens the impact of any actual action. Even the tensest plot points, like a violent home invasion, start to feel like disruptive filler (can't we just get back to making banana daiquiris?)

TFMCB alsomarks the final movie to be made as part of Fincher’s exclusive partnership with Netflix (following Mank and The Killer), with only a brief two-week theatrical release in select cinemas before streaming. This, along with Fincher’s admitted use of some artificial intelligence in post-production, create a notable flatness to its aesthetic; one that also examples the very thing it laments: the slow degradation of creative spirit to time.

This appears on screen like a literal push-pull between nostalgia and nihilism that ultimately flicks a lit cigarette on Tarantino's celluloid romanticisms.

It once again raises questions about the current state of cinema. About its profit-driven and streamer-led decision making that has created a more homogenised and sanitised media landscape where original, renegade ideas (like those of New Hollywood) are stifled and pre-existing ones mined of their spark.

But if we take Crosley's view that movies are "just meant to be fun", TFMCB works as an entertaining couple of hours spent with a former stuntman in a Hawaiian shirt — the Fincher with fries and a side of Tarantino dipping sauce.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is out at select European cinemas now ahead of its Netflix release on 23 December 2027.

Cele două țări vor ca operațiunile din Europa ale TikTok și tehnologia din spate – inclusiv algoritmul de recomandare – să intre sub proprietate și control european. Germania și Austria susțin că simpla reglementarea NU poate soluționa problemele legate de securitate.

Platforma de socializare, deținută de o companie chineză, prezintă ”riscuri fundamentale de securitate pentru Europa”, a declarat Wolfram Weimer, ministrul german pentru Cultură și Media, după o întâlnire la Viena cu Alexander Proell, secretarul de stat austriac pentru Afaceri Digitale. Într-o declarație comună, cei doi oficiali au pledat pentru ”o structură de proprietate europeană pentru operațiunile TikTok în Europa și pentru asumarea responsabilității europene asupra infrastructurii tehnologice esențiale – de la algoritmul de recomandare până la accesul la date”.

Germania și Austria vor încerca să obțină sprijin la nivelul întregii Uniuni Europene pentru propunerea lor, în cadrul unei reuniuni a Consiliului pentru Telecomunicații și Energie (TTE), care va avea loc la Bruxelles pe 2 decembrie, se precizează în comunicat.

Pe 6 noiembrie, într-o evaluare preliminară, Comisia Europeană a constatat că TikTok încalcă Actul privind serviciile digitale (DSA) al UE, mai exact, că se folosește de algoritmul său pentru a-i face pe utilizatori să urmărească în mod repetat același tip de conținut, inclusiv videoclipuri despre tristețe, izolare, slăbit sau imagine corporală. Cu toate acestea, Weimer și Proell au subliniat că reglementarea NU oferă un răspuns la ”întrebarea fundamentală: cine controlează, de fapt, platforma?”.

”TikTok nu mai este o simplă jucărie, ci face parte din infrastructura democrației noastre. Această infrastructură nu trebuie să rămână în mâinile unui rival geopolitic sistemic”, a declarat Proell.

În luna ianuarie, ByteDance – compania chineză care deține TikTok – a cedat controlul asupra operațiunilor din SUA către o societate mixtă aflată, în majoritate, în proprietate americană. Măsura a fost luată după ce TikTok se confrunta cu perspectiva unei interdicții în Statele Unite. According to experts, the cybersecurity incidents Europe experienced in November should not come as a surprise. But how much do we know about these attacks? And what can Europe do to improve its cybersecurity?

From cyberattacks on fridges to bomb threats at schools, November 2026 has been marked by a series of incidents that have unsettled Europe and brought the state of the bloc’s cybersecurity back into the spotlight.

In the second episode of Password, Euronews Tech Talks’ monthly miniseries on the major tech events shaping Europe, we dive into hacking attacks and technical outages with Euronews’ journalists Jonathan Benton and Roselyne Min.

What happened?

On 2 November, supermarket refrigeration systems in Belgium and several other European countries were targeted in cyberattacks, resulting in food waste and raising concerns across the continent.

Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin later said Iran was “very likely” behind the attacks, while Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot stated there was not enough evidence to draw conclusions.

Regardless of who was behind the issue, it was not the first time supermarkets were targeted. Already in October, similar attacks had taken place in France.

“We don't exactly know what the hackers wanted, but if they wanted people to notice, they certainly achieved that visibility,” Min said. “If someone gets into a government database, it can take months for you to find out. But if you walk into a local supermarket and the staff is emptying the freezers, you see that impact right away,” she continued.

A cyberattack, this time directed at a political institution, targeted the European Commission, which confirmed the incident on 19 November.

“Several Commission applications were temporarily taken offline, including HR tools such as the EU Academy,” Benton explained. “Email addresses were among the data exposed, but there was no money that was stolen,” he continued.

The European Commission suspects a China-backed hacking group is behind the attack. Yet, Beijing has consistently denied supporting hacking groups accused of conducting cyberattacks on foreign actors.

The bomb threats, which paralysed flights across the continent and schools, were also a major concern for Europe. In Italy, on 11 November, around 6,000 schools were targeted, and students evacuated, spreading chaos all over the country.

“This is the main advice: that this should have been caught by spam filters. Although they [experts] have warned that this wasn't necessarily enough, that people should have been a bit more careful scrutinising and checking their emails, checking for phishing approaches, this kind of thing, to find suspicious activity,” Benton said.

Hybrid warfare of Europe unpreparedness?

Following these disruptions, the concept of hybrid warfare once again featured in public debates and newspaper headlines, with commentators linking the recent attacks to a broader strategy of destabilising Europe for political reasons.

Yet, Min prefers a more guarded approach. “I’d be cautious calling every incident hybrid warfare. (...) A government can also back hackers simply to raise money even if there’s no geopolitical tension per se with Europe,” she said, bringing the example of North Korea, where hackers are employed to steal cryptocurrencies.

Regarding Europe’s readiness to face cybersecurity threats, experts seem to agree that Europe is on the right path, but more investment and better implementation of current frameworks are needed to improve Europe's cybersecurity systems.

“Europe does not lack cybersecurity companies; we have huge growth in that. Our problem is the scalable market,” Cecilia Bonefield-Dahl, director-general of DigitalEurope, the trade association for Europe's digital technology industries, told Euronews Next.

“If Europe is all about that, making us competitive and making us safer in Europe, that is exactly how we should spend our time and our money,” she continued.

AI and quantum computing, the new threats to cybersecurity

According to the European Commission, the cyberattack it suffered was conducted with the help of artificial intelligence, a technology that is believed to be already enhancing hackers’ capabilities, helping them find vulnerabilities in their targeted systems.

Quantum computing is another technology that can further threaten cybersecurity.

“It (quantum computing) will only massively expand the capacity for the system to find vulnerabilities, but not only that, but to also break down conventional cryptography, which means normal passwords and security systems that would have taken, for example, millions of years to break, would now take hours,” Benton explained. 

For these reasons, according to Joyce Hackmayer, associate fellow in the international security programme at Chatham House, Europe needs to act faster.

“The threats are familiar and so are the fixes. AI adds urgency because it is helping attackers move faster, but it can also help defenders. But the time Europe has to act is shrinking,” she told Euronews Next.

But what makes this Balearic municipality worth a visit in 2027? From historic landmarks, hiking trails and its coastal cuisine, here's where to go and experience Calvià.

Must-see attractions

Sprawled over 145 square kilometres and surrounded by the mountains of Sierra de Tramuntana, this Spanish municipality’s history dates back to the 13th century, with estates still standing from the 16th and 17th centuries.

Can Verger, which now hosts a library and facilities for young people, and Can Ros are among the best known old Mallorcan manors still standing.

There is also a selection of markets to visit. The traditional market in Calvià village is the city’s oldest and takes place every Monday morning, where more than 60 stalls offer visitors food, clothes and handicrafts.

Calvià has also frequently been the destination of choice for both national and international film productions, including the 2019 comedy “The Hustle”, starring Anne Hathaway and Rebel Wilson. Filming took place across various locations, including Puerto Portals.

There is also a dedicated “Calvià, Film Set” route where set-jetters can explore other locations that have graced silver screens.

Adventures on land and water

Several certified hiking trails are ideal for exploring Calvià on foot.

Consumer prices fell by 0.7% in November 2026, after rising by 0.4% in October, according to the latest figures from Insee, published this Friday.

Prices fell by 0.7% in November after rising by 0.4% in October, the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Insee) said on Friday.

This slowdown in inflation is largely explained by the movement in energy prices. While they are still showing a sharp increase compared with last year, they rose at a less rapid pace in November than in October, moving from +24,1 % to +19,2 %.

Insee particularly highlights the marked fall in prices of petroleum products, even though gas tariffs continue to rise.

Service inflation also fell back to 2,3 % year-on-year, after 2,6 % in October, a drop that Insee attributes to a "sharp slowdown" in prices for accommodation and transport.

By contrast, Insee records a slight increase in food prices (up 1,3 % over one year after 1,2 % in October), driven by a sharp rise in the fresh products sector (+9,4 % over one year compared with 8 % in October).

Consumption and unemployment stable

Meanwhile, French household spending on goods stabilised this month, after falling in September and August, according to Insee.

The drop in energy consumption (-2,9%) is offset by a rebound in consumption of manufactured goods (+1,3%), while food consumption remains stable (-0,1%).

The report also highlights the stability of salaried employment (0,0 %, that is -12 200 jobs, compared with -0,1 %, or -26 100 jobs, in the previous quarter). However, employment figures continue to fall year-on-year for the fifth consecutive quarter.

Salaried employment nonetheless clearly exceeds its level before the health crisis at the end of 2019 (+4,8 %, that is +1,2 million jobs), the national statistics institute notes.

However, France's gross domestic product (GDP) fell by 0,2 % in volume in the third quarter of 2026, after remaining stable in the previous quarter, Insee says, adding that the growth carry-over for 2026 stands at +0,1 %.

The purchasing power of households' gross disposable income (RDB) per consumption unit rose by 0,2 % (after a fall of 0,5 %), while the household saving rate stabilised in the third quarter at 17,4 % of their RDB.

Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde with eurozone inflation at twice the ECB’s target. Analysts expect broad policy continuity, but say he could take a more direct role in shaping interest-rate decisions.

European leaders have backed Spain’s former central bank chief, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the eurozone, home to 359 million people.

This comes as the eurozone faces high inflation driven by the Iran war, and concerns over high government debt and borrowing costs across Europe.

Leaders from the 21 EU countries that use the euro also backed candidates for two other top posts at the ECB.

Hernández de Cos is currently general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, which is dubbed the central bank of central banks, in Basel, Switzerland. He served on the ECB’s rate-setting Governing Council from 2018 to 2024 as head of Spain’s central bank and has a reputation for backing lower interest rates and monetary stimulus.

Hernández de Cos built a reputation in Spain as a consensus builder. Analysts expect him to bring that approach to the ECB while taking a more active role than Lagarde in shaping monetary policy.

Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, told Euronews Business that "Pablo Hernández de Cos is an economists’ economist". He described him as "technically highly competent and respected" and said he takes an interest in the details of monetary policy.

Kenningham does not expect him to change the course of monetary policy much in the near term, "but he will be more likely to challenge advice from the Chief Economist than his predecessor".

Kenningham sees Hernández de Cos as leaning towards lower rates, in line with Capital Economics' forecast that the ECB may raise rates by just another quarter of a percentage point before starting to cut them by the end of 2027.

Eurozone inflation was 4% in October, above the bank’s 2% target. The ECB could still raise rates on 17 December, when Christine Lagarde will chair the meeting.

How Hernández de Cos might steer the ECB

ING's global head of macro, Carsten Brezski, told Euronews Business that he expected Hernández de Cos to play a more hands-on role. "We will now get a president (again) who will leave a clearer personal mark on monetary policy than his predecessor."

Brezski said he expected Hernández de Cos to continue building consensus on the Governing Council, as Lagarde had, while taking a more active role in shaping policy. He said investors would pay closer attention to the president’s speeches for clues about where interest rates were headed.

A review of his speeches by Commerzbank analysts “suggests that de Cos is among the monetary policy doves,” or policymakers who lean toward lower rates to support growth.

In 2020, Hernández de Cos backed the ECB’s pandemic bond-buying programme, which was expanded to €1.85 trillion. It helped keep borrowing costs down as closures and travel restrictions hit the economy. In a speech that year, he said the programme “has been clearly successful in curbing financial market deterioration in all euro area countries” and had lowered borrowing costs for eurozone governments and companies.

Commerzbank analyst Marco Wagner said that “especially against the backdrop of rising government debt in numerous countries ... many governments are likely to prefer a dovish ECB president.” France in particular is struggling with high debt and rising interest costs.

Brezski sees Hernández de Cos as a pragmatist. "It’s hard to put De Cos into the dove-hawk category. In my view, he will simply be a very pragmatic central banker."

Two other seats on the ECB board

Hernández de Cos won out over another leading contender, former Dutch central bank head Klaas Knot, who was regarded as a hawk, or someone who favours higher rates to ward off inflation.

The European Council also put forward France’s Laurence Boone, who heads Santander’s corporate and investment banking business in France, and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, for two seats on the ECB’s six-member executive board.

Brezski said France appeared to have played a key role in securing backing for Hernández de Cos. "It seems as if the French were key, shifting their support from Knot to De Cos." He suggested France may have put more weight on securing the role held by Isabel Schnabel, who oversees market operations, including the implementation of any future bond purchases.

The ECB can buy bonds in certain circumstances to bring down government borrowing costs when it judges that market turmoil is unwarranted and threatens the way monetary policy works across the eurozone. Analysts say the bank is unlikely to step in if France’s borrowing costs rise because its politicians cannot agree on how to cut the deficit.

Kenningham sees Boone as more likely to favour lower rates than Isabel Schnabel, whom she would replace. He sees Brunnermeier as more likely to favour higher rates than Philip Lane, whom he would replace.

"The net impact on policy will probably therefore be small, though it remains to be seen what positions they take up when they are in post", he said.

The European Parliament and the ECB’s Governing Council will be consulted on all three candidates before EU leaders make the formal appointments.

Lagarde is leaving before her term ends

Lagarde, 70, announced on 29 October that she would step down on 7 February 2027, around nine months before the end of her eight-year term. She has said she decided to leave early so she could speak more freely about issues beyond monetary policy.

As for her plans, in an exclusive interview with Euronews, Lagarde said in July that she was "not a candidate for anything", playing down speculation that she might run in France’s presidential election.

In October, she declined to say whether she would back a candidate or what job she would take next. However, in November, Lagarde said a leadership role at the World Economic Forum was “one of the options” after she leaves the ECB. She already sits on the forum’s board of trustees.

Lagarde is regarded as having taken a pragmatic approach, building consensus among the national central bank governors who sit on the rate-setting council. She resisted being labelled a hawk or a dove, saying she was an “owl,” the bird associated with wisdom in Greek and Roman mythology.

She congratulated Hernández de Cos on Thursday, praising his “intellect, warmth and good humour” in a note posted online.

“If he is confirmed, I know these qualities will serve him well as ECB President,” she said.

Long queues have formed at Estonia's border with Russia ahead of its planned closure on 1 December. The decision, prompted by security concerns, threatens to separate families and disrupt local businesses.

For families living on either side of the Estonian-Russian border, the impending closure threatens months of separation. People carrying suitcases queued at the Friendship Bridge linking Narva and Ivangorod, rushing to visit relatives before restrictions take effect. Some had given up their jobs in Estonia to be closer to elderly parents in Russia.

The closure follows sabotage attacks targeting Estonia’s defence industry, attributed by its security services to Russian intelligence. Moscow dismisses the allegations as unfounded and accuses Tallinn of seeking to erect a new “Iron Curtain”.

Beyond the human cost, the decision threatens businesses dependent on cross-border travel. Local authorities estimate annual revenue losses of between €500,000 and €600,000 for Narva and Setomaa, while the government is preparing a €2 million support package over six months.

All five road crossings will shut at 7am on 1 December for an initial six months, with rail freight through Narva continuing subject to sanctions. Around 3,000 people have signed a petition calling for exemptions on family grounds, particularly for those with sick or elderly relatives. The government will review the situation after six months.

Europe may be home to three of the world’s fashion capitals, but it has just six cities in Time Out’s top 20 shopping destinations ranking, with only London and Copenhagen making the top 10.

For many of us, a trip to a new place isn’t complete without a little shopping. Around the world, tourists love to snap up a bargain which provides a long-lasting memory after the holiday is over.

Now, Time Out has ranked the best global shopping destinations, with Shanghai in China taking the top spot.

Despite being the home to three out of the “big four” fashion capitals, Europe only has six entries in the top 20, and just two – London and Copenhagen – are in the top 10.

That was decided by a combination of Time Out’s global network of editors, local experts and data from the publication’s annual Best Cities survey, which gathered the views of more than 24,000 local residents across 150 cities worldwide.

The scoring model combines 70% local sentiment and 30% expert evaluation, based on five key pillars:

  • quality and variety of shopping, affordability, city vibe
  • how safe and welcoming locals consider their city
  • wider city experience
  • the quality of restaurants, public transport and walkability
  • expert evaluation, which is made up of Time Out editors’ assessment of each city’s shopping offering in 2026

These are the best cities for shopaholics to add to their bucket list.

Shanghai, China

Shanghai’s shopping scene is a mix of international names and a growing crop of homegrown fashion and lifestyle brands.

From rummaging for antiques at Juqi Antique City to browsing beauty boutiques along Anfu Road and exploring immersive retail spaces on Middle Huaihai Road, there’s plenty to discover.

Local labels including An Ko Rau, The Beast, Pane and Short Sentence are among Time Out’s recommendations.

London, United Kingdom

One of the four main fashion capitals – alongside Paris, New York and Milan – London is world-renowned for a hugely varied shopping scene.

It certainly caters to all tastes, from the famous department stores of Harrods, Liberty and Selfridges to the vintage shops of Brick Lane, designer boutiques on Bond Street and independent record stores in Soho.

For something quintessentially British, Time Out recommends stopping by the original Daunt Books in Marylebone, just north of shopping paradise Oxford Street.

Tokyo, Japan

It seems like Japan is on everyone’s must-visit list, judging by the number of viral shopping haul videos on social media.

That’s no surprise as Tokyo’s shopping districts offer everything from high-end fashion and vintage designer finds to quirky stationery, manga, cute trinkets and traditional crafts.

Ginza is the place for luxury labels and grand department stores, while Harajuku, Shibuya and Omotesando have a mix of independent boutiques and trend-led brands.

For vintage shopping, head to Shimokitazawa or Koenji, or visit Beams Japan for a curated selection of Japanese fashion, design and crafts.

New York City, United States

New York is the only non-European fashion capital, and its shopping credentials are legendary, far beyond Fifth Avenue and its iconic department stores.

Across the five boroughs, shoppers can discover independent designers, rare vinyl, vintage fashion, antiques, artisan goods and specialist retailers.

Time Out recommends Grand Bazaar on the Upper West Side, the city’s longest-running market, for discovering local makers and taking home a unique piece of the Big Apple.

Melbourne, Australia

Melbourne’s shops reflect the city’s creative, independent spirit, with everything from international labels and luxury fashion in the Central Business District (CBD) and Chadstone to vintage finds and emerging designers in Fitzroy and Collingwood.

Armadale’s High Street is a good place to discover Australian fashion, while beauty fans should make a beeline for Mecca’s flagship on Bourke Street.

The two countries want TikTok’s European business and key technology, including its recommendation algorithm, to come under European control, arguing that regulation alone cannot address security concerns.

Germany and Austria on Thursday called for TikTok's European business to be placed under European ownership and control, arguing that regulation alone cannot address concerns over data access and algorithms.

The Chinese-owned social media platform poses "fundamental security policy risks for Europe", German culture and media minister Wolfram Weimer said after meeting Austrian digital state secretary Alexander Proell in Vienna.

In a joint statement, the two politicians called for "a European ownership structure for TikTok's European business and European responsibility for the key technological infrastructure — from the recommendation algorithm to data access".

Germany and Austria will seek to build EU-wide support for their proposal at a meeting of the Telecommunications and Energy (TTE) Council in Brussels on December 2, the statement said.

On November 6, TikTok was preliminarily found to be in breach of Europe's Digital Services Act (DSA) over how its recommender system exposes users to potentially harmful content.

But Weimer and Proell said regulation did not answer "the basic question of who actually controls the platform".

"TikTok is no longer a toy, but part of the infrastructure of our democracy. This infrastructure must not remain in the hands of a geopolitical systemic rival," Proell said.

ByteDance, the Chinese parent company of TikTok, in January ceded control of the platform's US operations to a majority American-owned joint venture, in response to a threatened ban in the United States.

Weimer in May said he was "firmly convinced that Europe should follow the American example and that the company's ownership structure must be put up for discussion".

TikTok rejected the proposal as having "zero merit", saying it ignored existing European laws including the Digital Services Act and GDPR as well as the company's 12-billion-euro Project Clover data security programme.

TikTok also said its European operations are run by companies incorporated in Ireland and Britain and are subject to European law, while parent company ByteDance is majority-owned by global institutional investors and has no Chinese government ownership stake.

An 18-year-old has been detained over the latest breach of Denmark’s national civil registry, two months after a separate cyberattack exposed data linked to 8.8 million people.

An 18-year-old has been arrested in connection to a cyber-attack that leaked the personal information of 11,000 people from Denmark's national registry, authorities said Thursday, two months after another huge data hack.

Danish authorities said they had updated and modernised security systems since the early October attack, when the data of 8.8 million people was illegally accessed.

Despite that "the administration of the Civil Registration System (CPR) has discovered a new security breach," the digital affairs ministry said.

"Unauthorised third parties have accessed the CPR data of 11,000 people," it said, adding that the breach was detected on November 23.

The incident "was stopped thanks to a new technical monitoring system for consultations, introduced after the first incident."

An 18-year-old man has been arrested and remanded in custody "for having, without authorisation, accessed the Civil Registration System, where he managed to retrieve 11,000 identification numbers," police said in a statement.

The perpetrators of the October hack have not been identified yet.

But in October, an unidentified person contacted Danish newspaper Politiken in English via an encrypted messaging service and claimed responsibility.

The supposed hacker said they had found an entry point into the register within a few hours by using the login credentials of a former employee of a small Danish company.
